headline: Yakuwari is 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) plus 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).
Moeru is from the classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu), by way of moju and mojeru.
Ōu is the Old Japanese verb 覆ふ (opu, “cover from above”) plus ふ (-fu), which expresses repetition or ongoing state.
Tō, “tower”, abbreviates 卒塔婆 (sotoba), a transliteration of Sanskrit stūpa, “heap”.
Su, “nest”, is found in the Kojiki of 712, from Proto-Japonic *su.
Chii is from Middle Chinese 地位, first cited in Japanese in the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing.
Sensu is first attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.
Hitomi is likely 人 (hito, “person”) plus 見 (mi, “see”): one's own reflection in someone else's eyes.
Urusai is probably 心 (uru, “heart, mind”) plus 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”): something so overwhelming that one feels pressured.
Kaeru, “to change”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu).
Oba, an aunt, is likely 小 (o-, “small, young”) plus 母 (ha, “mother”), as 叔父 (oji) is 小 plus 父.
Chūshajō is 駐車 (chūsha, “(car) parking”) plus 場 (-jō, “place”).
Tadaima is short for 只今、帰りました (tadaima, kaerimashita), “I'm back right now”.
Mukai is the continuative stem of 向かう (mukau, “to face”).
In hōtai, 包 is a daiyōji replacing 繃.
Fushi was pusi in Old Japanese, attested in 794 as 布之.
Hizuke is 日 (hi, “day”) plus 付け (-zuke, “fixing, attaching”).
Miokuru is 見 (mi, “seeing”) plus 送る (okuru, “to send”).
Nobiru, “to be prolonged”, is from the classical upper bigrade verb のぶ, cognate with 伸びる (nobiru).
Uranau is from 裏 (ura, “back, inside”) or 心 (ura, “heart”), plus なふ (nau, verb modifier).
This nobiru, written 伸, shares its classical verb のぶ (nobu) with 延びる (nobiru).
Totemo is a clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”); the sense “very” is a later shift, first attested around 1910-1920.
Yorokobi is the continuative stem of 喜ぶ (yorokobu, “to be pleased, delighted”).
Kyū ni is 急 (kyū, “sudden”) plus に (ni, oblique particle).
Suruto is する (suru, “to do”) plus と (to): literally “when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]”.
Kaeru, “to return”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapyaru.
Nikui is cognate with 憎む (nikumu, “to hate”).
Daga is だ (da, “is, are”, copula) plus が (ga).
Sono is そ, the distal demonstrative root of Old Japanese, plus の (no).
In chūmon, 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.
Saitei is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 低 (tei, “low”).
